entries.modern_form: PIE *(s)kel- 'to bend; crooked' (Pokorny 928, lemma '(s)kel-4'; Watkins/AHD 'skel-3. Also kel-. Crooked')
entries.note: The root is real and correctly labelled. Pokorny IEW 928 has "Root / lemma: (s)kel-4 (extended klā-, klō-) / Meaning: to bend; crooked", with the Greek family σκέλος, σκελλός, σκολιός, σκώληξ, κελλόν, κυλλός, κυλίνδω, κῶλον; Walde-Pokorny II 597-598 is the same article ('4. sqel- krumm', which is Pokorny's own cross-reference 'WP. II 597 ff.'); Watkins prints "skel-3. Also kel-. Crooked. With derivatives referring to a bent or curved part of the body, such as a leg, heel, knee, or hip. [Pok. 4. skel- 928.]" Nourai's numbering 'Skel 1' is his own (it is Pokorny's fourth (s)kel-); his gloss 'bent, curved' is right, and his redirect 'Skel 2 -> Sek' takes care of the homonymous 'cut' root. Two weaknesses run through the chart rather than the root box: (i) the Greek reflexes κυλίνδειν and κῶλον are attached to this root only 'quite doubtfully' (Watkins) or 'probably' (Klein), and Beekes prefers Pre-Greek for κῶλον; (ii) the box for Greek 'kôlon' silently merges the unrelated homonym κόλον 'large intestine', which is what carries the Arabic/Persian قولون branch. One printing error: the Greek node #4 'skhelos' should read skellos (σκελλός).
entries.note_fa: ریشه اصیل است و برچسبِ زبانی و معنای آن درست. پوکورنی (فرهنگ ریشه‌شناختی هندواروپایی، ص ۹۲۸) سرواژهٔ «(s)kel-4 (با گسترشِ klā-, klō-)» را با معنای «خم شدن؛ کج» می‌آورد و خانوادهٔ یونانیِ σκέλος، σκελλός، σκολιός، σκώληξ، κελλόν، κυλλός، κυλίνδω و κῶλον را زیر آن می‌نشاند؛ والده-پوکورنی (ج۲ صص ۵۹۷–۵۹۸) همان مقاله است (خودِ پوکورنی به «WP. II 597 ff.» ارجاع می‌دهد) و واتکینز در پیوستِ AHD می‌نویسد: «skel-3، همچنین kel-. کج. با مشتقاتی که به اندامِ خمیدهٔ تن — ساق، پاشنه، زانو، ران — اشاره دارند». شمارهٔ «Skel 1» از خودِ نورایی است (نزد پوکورنی چهارمین (s)kel- است) و ارجاعِ «Skel 2 ← Sek» هم‌آواییِ «بریدن» را جدا می‌کند. دو سستی در بدنهٔ چارت هست نه در جعبهٔ ریشه: نخست آنکه κυλίνδειν و κῶλον تنها «با تردیدِ بسیار» (واتکینز) یا «احتمالاً» (کلاین) به این ریشه بسته شده‌اند و بیکس برای κῶλον خاستگاهِ پیشایونانی را ترجیح می‌دهد؛ دوم آنکه جعبهٔ «kôlon» هم‌آوایِ بی‌ربطِ κόλον «رودهٔ بزرگ» را در خود ادغام کرده و همین معنا است که شاخهٔ «قولون» عربی و فارسی را حمل می‌کند. یک خطای چاپی نیز هست: در گرهٔ ۴ باید skellos (σκελλός) خوانده شود نه skhelos.

Attributed (quite doubtfully) by some to this root is Greek kulindein, to roll: CALENDER, CYLINDER. [Pok. 4. skel- 928.]"

Mann's cross-reference "skelos, see skhelos and cf. skel- (3)" routes the Greek leg-word to a lemma he glosses 'wrong, fraud' — his arrangement of the (s)kel- homonyms differs from Pokorny's and does not support the chart's gloss.

nodes.derivation: شل šal 'thigh, (upper) leg' is the Persian member of the root: Wiktionary's Etymology 2 for شل ('thigh of a man; thin coloured leather') takes it back to PIE *skelo-, i.e. exactly Pokorny's (s)kel- 928, and names شلوار as its derivative. Horn, Grundriss no. 789 (p.175) heads the entry "šal 'Schenkel', šeleng (šileng); vergl. šalvār 'Hosen'" and equates it with Gk. σκέλος (after Justi), while warning that Armenian srunk 'shins' does NOT belong here. شلنگ šelang 'stride, leap' is šal + the denominal suffix -ang; Borhan-e Qate' (printed 1286) defines it 'برجستن و فروجستن شاطران ... جهت ورزش و مشق راه رفتن' — the leaping and striding of couriers done as exercise, which is precisely Nourai's double gloss 'step, also a leg exercise'. شلوار is the weak link: Horn himself says 'np. šalvār ist weit entlehnt' and lists Gk. σαράβαρα (Photius, Pollux), Arab. sarbāl/sirwāl, Kurd. šelvār, Oss. salbaro, Wakhi savālak; modern work (Cheung, Iranian Borrowings in Qur'ānic Arabic, 2017, via Wiktionary) derives NP شلوار from MP šalwār (Book Pahlavi šlwʾl), itself a borrowing from Proto-Scythian *šalawāri, tentatively analysed *šali 'leg, thigh' (the cognate of Persian šal) + *wāri 'covering' (< PIr. *wā́rah-). So Nourai's paraphrase '"like legs", pants' matches the modern internal analysis of the compound, but the word reached Persian from Scythian/Saka — via Achaemenid Elamite šá-ir-ba-la-ad-da and Aramaic/Syriac — rather than being built inside Persian from šal. شلپوی šalpǔy 'the sound of footsteps' is real (Asadi, Loghat-e Fors p.207; the Bū-Shakūr Balkhī couplet the chart quotes), but Borhan records it beside the variants شکپوی and شگپوی, so its first element is not securely šal 'leg'; attaching it to this root is Nourai's own step and is unsupported.
nodes.derivation_fa: «شَل» به معنی ران و پای، بازماندهٔ ایرانی باستان *šala- و از ریشهٔ هندواروپایی آغازین *skelo- «کج، خمیده؛ اندام خمیدهٔ تن» است و هم‌ریشهٔ σκέλος یونانی «ران» شمرده می‌شود (هرن، شمارهٔ ۷۸۹؛ ویکی‌واژه). «شلنگ» از شل + پسوند ـنگ ساخته شده و برهان قاطع (ص ۱۲۸۶) آن را «برجستن و فروجستن شاطران ... جهت ورزش و مشق راه رفتن» تعریف می‌کند که درست همان معنای دوگانهٔ نورایی است. اما «شلوار» وام‌واژه است نه ساختِ درونیِ فارسی: خودِ هرن می‌نویسد که این واژه «بسیار وام داده شده» (σαράβαρα یونانی، سِروال/سِربال عربی، شلوار کردی، salbaro آسی) و پژوهش امروزی (چونگ ۲۰۱۷) آن را از فارسی میانهٔ šalwār و آن را وام‌گرفته از سکایی آغازین *šalawāri می‌داند که احتمالاً از *šali «ران» + *wāri «پوشش» ساخته شده است؛ یعنی تحلیل معناییِ نورایی («مانندِ پاها») درست است ولی راهِ ورود واژه به فارسی از راه سکایی بوده است. «شلپوی» نیز در لغت فرس (ص ۲۰۷) و برهان با گونه‌های «شکپوی» و «شگپوی» آمده، پس جزء نخست آن به‌یقین «شل» نیست و پیوند دادنش به این ریشه از خودِ نورایی است. نتیجه: ادعای نورایی دربارهٔ «شل» و «شلنگ» درست است و دربارهٔ «شلوار» و «شلپوی» با احتیاط پذیرفتنی است.

nodes.derivation: Ancient Greek σκέλος (skélos), n., 'leg, thigh' (Homer onwards), is a s-stem *skel-es- built directly on the root: Watkins reconstructs "Suffixed form *skel-es- in Greek skelos, leg", and Pokorny 928 opens the Greek material of (s)kel-4 with "Gr. skelos m. 'thigh'" beside σκελίς 'hind foot, haunch' and σκολιός 'crooked'. The semantics are the root's own: the leg is named as the bending limb.

nodes.derivation: English isosceles (1550s, of a triangle with two equal sides) is Latin isoscelēs, a straight borrowing of Greek ἰσοσκελής isoskelḗs 'equal-legged' = ἴσος 'equal' + σκέλος 'leg' — the triangle's two equal sides being felt as its two legs. Klein: "isosceles, adj. ... L., fr. Gk. isoskeles, 'equal-legged', fr. isos, 'equal', and skelos, 'leg'"; Watkins lists ISOSCELES (with TRISKELION) under skel-3 §2. A learned borrowing through Latin, with no intermediate vernacular stage.

nodes.derivation: Both words are real Greek, but the first is misspelt. Walde-Pokorny II 598 — the page Nourai cites as WLD:597, where the root '4. sqel- krumm' begins — lists, side by side, σκελλός (skellós) glossed 'διεστραμμένος, pandus, scaurus' (twisted, bandy-legged) and the Hesychian gloss κελλόν· στρεβλόν, πλάγιον (kellón 'crooked, slanting'); Pokorny 928 repeats both ("skellos 'bowlegged' ... kellon streblon, plagion Hes."). There is no Greek word *σχελος / skhelos meaning 'crooked'; the printed page of Nourai shows 'skhelos, kellos', so the -h- is the book's own slip for skellos (the doubled -ll- misread or mistyped as -lh-). The chart's second form 'kellos' is the Hesychian neuter κελλόν cited in the masculine nominative, which is a normalisation rather than an error. With those two corrections the node is sound: both are o-grade/zero-grade adjectives of *(s)kel- meaning 'bent, crooked'. Note also that S. E. Mann's Indo-European Comparative Dictionary does have a lemma spelt 'skhelos', but it means 'wrong, fraud' (Lat. scelus, Skt. chalaḥ) and belongs to a different (s)kel- root — so that lemma cannot rescue the chart's gloss 'crooked'.

nodes.derivation: The Persian word is genuine and does belong to this root, but not as a descendant of Greek. کَل kol/kul 'crooked, curved' is listed by Walde-Pokorny II 598 inside the sqel- 'krumm' article itself — "np. kul 'krumm, gekrümmt' (s. Hübschmann Arm. Gr. I 457)" — i.e. as an independent Iranian cognate; Horn no. 861 (p.192) does the same: "861. kul 'krumm, gekrümmt'. Nach Nöldeke zu gr. κυλλός 'krumm'", adding that Fortunatov instead linked κυλλός to Skt. kuṇi- 'lame in the arm' (< *kulni-), which would loosen the tie. Moʿin's Farhang has the headword کل with the bracketed etymological gloss '[کج؛ منحنی]' and the definition 'منحنی، کج. کجی، انحنا'. So the word, the meaning and the root membership are all confirmed; what is wrong is the arrow: the chart hangs Persian kol under the Greek box, which would make it a Greek loanword, whereas every source treats it as a sister form inherited in Iranian (PIE *kul-no- / *kel- beside Gk. κυλλός). Nourai's own layout elsewhere uses this position for cognates, so this is probably a diagram artefact rather than a claim of borrowing — but as drawn it is wrong.

nodes.derivation: Greek κυλίνδειν (kylíndein) 'to roll, roll up' (with the nouns κύλινδρος 'roller, cylinder', κυλίνδρα) is a real and well-attested verb, but its attachment to *(s)kel- is precisely the doubtful link of this article, and Nourai's chart gives no hint of that. Watkins states it with an explicit warning: "6. Attributed (quite doubtfully) by some to this root is Greek kulindein, to roll: CALENDER, CYLINDER." Pokorny 928 does list "kulindo, -eo 'rolle, walze' (Ionian Attic kalindeo), kulindros 'Walze, pulley, Zylinder'" under (s)kel-4, and Klein says only "prob. derives fr. I.-E. base *(s)qel 'to bend, twist'". Etymonline/Beekes call the verb's origin simply unknown, and a rival tradition connects it to *kʷel- 'turn' (the κύκλος family). Formally the ku- vocalism is the same problem as in κυλλός, for which Pokorny has to posit a 'reduced grade' *kul-. So: root, language and gloss are right; the edge root→kulindein is accepted by some and doubted by others.

nodes.derivation: The chart merges two different Greek words into one box. (a) κῶλον kōlon (long o, omega) 'limb, member (of a body); member of a clause' is the one Watkins and Pokorny put here — "Suffixed lengthened-grade form *kōl-o- in Greek kōlon, limb, member: COLON(1)" — and it is the source of the punctuation colon of node #14; Klein adds the related κωλέα, κωλῆ 'thighbone' and cognate OCS koleno 'knee'. Even that much is now contested: Beekes (via Wiktionary) prefers a Pre-Greek origin for κῶλον. (b) κόλον kólon (short o, omicron) 'large intestine' is a wholly separate word: Wiktionary states flatly "No relation to κῶλον (kôlon, 'limb')", its origin is uncertain (Beekes links it to words for 'guts'), and it is the word that gave Latin cōlon 'colon (anatomy)', Syriac ܩܘܠܘܢ qōlōn and hence Arabic قولون. Klein and Skeat both keep the two apart in separate entries (Klein: "colon, n., that part of the larger intestine ... fr. Gk. kolon, 'large intestine', which is of uncertain origin"). So the gloss 'limb, part, member' is supported by Nourai's own reference AHD, but the added 'large intestine' imports an unrelated homonym — and that sense is what carries the whole Arabic/Persian branch below.

nodes.derivation: Pass-through node for the Arabic medical vocabulary. The Arabic forms are قُولُون qūlūn 'the colon' and قُولَنْج qūlanj 'colic', both Greek loans that entered Arabic with the ninth-century Baghdad translations of Galen and Hippocrates — normally through Syriac, where Classical Syriac ܩܘܠܘܢ qōlōn is attested as the direct descendant of Greek κόλον; qūlanj renders Greek κωλικός/κολικός 'of the colon, colic'. Al-ʿUnaysī's Tafsīr al-alfāẓ al-dākhila (TAD), the reference Nourai cites, has the entry: 'قولنج ... مرض يصيب القولون ... [من] اليوناني الذي معناه شعبة من الأمعاء الغلاظ ... وهو في الأعور والمستقيم' — a disease affecting the colon, from the Greek word meaning a section of the thick intestines. nodes.derivation: Pass-through node for the Latin stage. Latin cōlon, -ī n. is a learned borrowing of Greek κῶλον, taken into Roman rhetorical writing (Cicero, Quintilian) in the technical sense 'a member of a period, a clause of a sentence' — and, as the metrical term, 'part of a verse'. (Latin also has the homonym colon 'large intestine', separately borrowed from Greek κόλον; that one feeds the medical vocabulary, not the punctuation word.) From the rhetorical Latin word, via the sixteenth-century printers' use of the term for the mark that sets off such a clause, comes English colon at node #14.

nodes.derivation: colon (the punctuation mark) is first recorded in the 1540s, from Latin colon 'part of a verse or poem, clause', from Greek κῶλον 'limb, member; clause of a sentence'; the sense went 'limb' > 'clause' > 'the mark that sets a clause off'. semicolon (1640s) is a hybrid formed in English by prefixing Latin semi- 'half' to that colon, for a stop half as strong. nodes.derivation: The Avestan word is real but its root is not this one on the modern view. Bartholomae, Altiranisches Wörterbuch col. 1745, gives "j., g. haxt- n. 'der innere Teil des Oberschenkels'" (the inner part of the thigh, Vd. 8.59, F. 3g), citing Skt. sakthi- and Ossetic aγd 'loin' — note that the stem is haxt-, and that Bartholomae's own footnote warns "haxt- und ai. sakthi- decken sich nicht" and suggests the Iranian -t- may be due to the influence of ast- 'bone' and srōni- 'hip'. Pokorny 930, the reference Nourai cites, does equate them and reconstructs *skn̥g-ti- ('Old Indic sakthi- n. (= Avestan haxti-) "thigh" (*skak-thi-, IE *skng-ti-)'), so Nourai reproduces his source faithfully. But that equation is now abandoned: Walde-Pokorny II 564 did not have it; Mann's Indo-European Comparative Dictionary puts the pair under a different lemma *soghtis 'thigh' (root segh-/sogh- 'hold'); Wiktionary's own (s)keng- page lists only khañjati, skázō, Germanic *skankô, Celtic *kengeti and Slavic *šęgati — no Iranian — while sakthi-/haxti- are placed under PIE *sokʷHt-i-s 'thigh'. nodes.derivation: English shank is inherited, not borrowed: Old English sc(e)anca 'leg, shin, shank (the part between knee and ankle)' > Middle English schanke, shanke > shank, with the regular Old English palatalisation of sc- to /ʃ/ before a front vowel and the loss of the weak final -a. Old English sceanca continues Proto-West Germanic *skankō < Proto-Germanic *skankô, and so goes back to *(s)keng- 'to limp, be askew'; the cognates are Dutch schenkel, German Schenkel, Danish/Swedish skank, West Frisian skonk. Watkins and Klein both give exactly this line, and Etymonline adds the semantic note that the Germanic noun literally means 'that which bends'. Worth recording as a historical curiosity: Skeat's Concise Dictionary (1911 ed.) still derived shank from A.S. sceacan 'to shake' — "named from its motion in running; lit. 'shaker'" — a folk-etymological explanation that no modern authority keeps.
nodes.derivation_fa: واژهٔ انگلیسیِ shank موروثی است نه وام‌واژه: انگلیسیِ کهنِ sc(e)anca «ساق، پا، بخشِ میانِ زانو و قوزک» ← انگلیسیِ میانهٔ schanke/shanke ← shank، با کام‌شدگیِ قاعده‌مندِ sc- به /ʃ/ پیش از واکهٔ پیشین و افتادنِ ـa پایانی. صورتِ انگلیسیِ کهن بازماندهٔ ژرمنیِ باختریِ آغازینِ *skankō و ژرمنیِ آغازینِ *skankô است و از این راه به ریشهٔ *(s)keng- «لنگیدن، کج بودن» می‌رسد؛ هم‌ریشه‌های آن schenkel هلندی، Schenkel آلمانی، skank دانمارکی و سوئدی و skonk فریزیِ باختری‌اند. واتکینز و کلاین همین زنجیره را می‌آورند و اتیمانلاین می‌افزاید که معنای تحت‌اللفظیِ نامِ ژرمنی «آنچه خم می‌شود» است. یک نکتهٔ تاریخی شایانِ ثبت: اسکیت در ویراستِ ۱۹۱۱ فرهنگ فشردهٔ خود هنوز shank را از sceacan «لرزیدن، تکان دادن» می‌گرفت («از حرکتش هنگام دویدن نام گرفته؛ به‌معنی تحت‌اللفظی: لرزاننده») — ریشه‌شناسیِ عامیانه‌ای که هیچ مرجعِ امروزی آن را نگه نداشته است. ادعای نورایی درست است.

"skeng-. Crooked. Germanic *skankon-, 'that which bends,' leg, in Old English sc(e)anca, shinbone: SHANK. [Pok. (s)keng- 930.]" — Watkins's entry is confined to the Germanic branch; he lists no Indo-Iranian reflex.

consulted.note: "shank, lower part of the leg. (E.) A.S. sceanca, scanca, bone of the leg; named from its motion in running; lit. 'shaker'. — A.S. sceacan, to shake, also to run. + Du. schonk, Dan. skank, Swed. skank, Low G. schunke, leg." Skeat's derivation from 'shake' is superseded; his cognate list is the same as everyone else's.
